claim: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is the commonest cause of congenital infection.
source: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is the commonest cause of congenital infection and particularly so among infants born to HIV-infected women.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about CMV.

claim: CMV is particularly common among infants born to HIV-infected women.
source: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is the commonest cause of congenital infection and particularly so among infants born to HIV-infected women.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact.

claim: Anatomic CMV compartmentalization was demonstrated in five HIV-infected mothers.
source: Using newly developed tools to reconstruct CMV haplotypes, we demonstrate anatomic CMV compartmentalization in five HIV-infected mothers and identify the possibility of congenitally transmitted genotypes in three of their infants.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on haplotype reconstruction analysis.

claim: Congenitally transmitted genotypes were identified in three infants.
source: Using newly developed tools to reconstruct CMV haplotypes, we demonstrate anatomic CMV compartmentalization in five HIV-infected mothers and identify the possibility of congenitally transmitted genotypes in three of their infants.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on sequencing and haplotype analysis.

claim: A single CMV strain was transmitted in each congenitally infected case.
source: A single CMV strain was transmitted in each congenitally infected case, and all were closely related to those that predominate in the cognate maternal cervix.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on haplotype analysis of infant samples.

claim: Congenitally transmitted CMV strains were closely related to those that predominate in the maternal cervix.
source: A single CMV strain was transmitted in each congenitally infected case, and all were closely related to those that predominate in the cognate maternal cervix.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on comparison of maternal cervical and infant CMV sequences.

claim: Congenitally transmitted CMV strains showed statistically significant similarities in 19 genes associated with tissue tropism and immunomodulation compared to non-transmitted strains.
source: Compared to non-transmitted strains, these congenitally transmitted CMV strains showed statistically significant similarities in 19 genes associated with tissue tropism and immunomodulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on FST analysis comparing transmitted and non-transmitted strains.

claim: All infants experienced incident superinfections with distinct strains from breast milk during follow-up.
source: In all infants, incident superinfections with distinct strains from breast milk were captured during follow-up.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on longitudinal sequencing of infant samples.

claim: Between 0.2% and 2% of all live births have congenital CMV infection (cCMVi).
source: Between 0.2% and 2% of all live births have congenital CMV infection (cCMVi), and of these, an estimated 15–20% develop permanent sequelae ranging from sensorineural hearing loss to severe neurocognitive impairment (Boppana et al., 2013; Dollard et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: An estimated 15–20% of infants with congenital CMV infection develop permanent sequelae ranging from sensorineural hearing loss to severe neurocognitive impairment.
source: Between 0.2% and 2% of all live births have congenital CMV infection (cCMVi), and of these, an estimated 15–20% develop permanent sequelae ranging from sensorineural hearing loss to severe neurocognitive impairment (Boppana et al., 2013; Dollard et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Maternal coinfection with HIV is associated with higher CMV viral loads in plasma, saliva, cervix, and breast milk.
source: Maternal coinfection with HIV, even when mitigated by antiretroviral treatment, is associated with higher CMV viral loads in plasma, saliva, cervix, and breast milk, and a greater risk of both congenital and postnatal CMV transmission (Gantt et al., 2016a; Gantt et al., 2016b; Slyker et al., 2017; Richardson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Maternal coinfection with HIV is associated with a greater risk of both congenital and postnatal CMV transmission.
source: Maternal coinfection with HIV, even when mitigated by antiretroviral treatment, is associated with higher CMV viral loads in plasma, saliva, cervix, and breast milk, and a greater risk of both congenital and postnatal CMV transmission (Gantt et al., 2016a; Gantt et al., 2016b; Slyker et al., 2017; Richardson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Primary maternal CMV infection during pregnancy confers a 30–40% risk of transmission to the foetus.
source: Primary maternal CMV infection during pregnancy confers a 30–40% risk of transmission to the foetus (Kenneson and Cannon, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Pre-existing maternal CMV immunity appears to reduce the risk of congenital CMV infection, though it is clearly imperfect.
source: Pre-existing maternal CMV immunity appears to reduce the risk of cCMVi, though it is clearly imperfect (Britt, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Over two-thirds of infants with congenital CMV infection are born to seropositive women.
source: Over two-thirds of infants with cCMVi are born to seropositive women, which constitute 88.4% of women in the Kenyan community from whom these study participants were drawn (Maingi and Nyamache, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: 88.4% of women in the Kenyan community from which study participants were drawn are CMV seropositive.
source: Over two-thirds of infants with cCMVi are born to seropositive women, which constitute 88.4% of women in the Kenyan community from whom these study participants were drawn (Maingi and Nyamache, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The overall risk of congenital CMV infection is directly proportional to the maternal seroprevalence in a population.
source: Moreover, the overall risk of cCMVi is directly proportional to the maternal seroprevalence in a population (de Vries et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Maternal CMV reinfection with new antigenic strains during pregnancy is a major risk factor for non-primary congenital CMV infection.
source: Increasing evidence points to the importance of maternal CMV reinfection with new antigenic strains during pregnancy as a major risk factor for non-primary cCMVi (Britt, 2017; Boppana et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Household children may be a source of maternal CMV reinfection.
source: Evidence that household children may be a source of maternal reinfection provides additional support for this hypothesis (Boucoiran et al., 2018; Barbosa et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The CMV genome is the largest of the human herpesviruses.
source: The CMV genome is the largest of the human herpesviruses.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about CMV.

claim: Regions of extensive sequence variability, together with high levels of recombination between different strains, result in high diversity for a DNA virus.
source: Regions of extensive sequence variability, together with high levels of recombination between different strains, result in high diversity for a DNA virus (Lassalle et al., 2016; Pokalyuk et al., 2017; Sackman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Individuals are often infected with multiple CMV strains.
source: Individuals are often infected with multiple CMV strains.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about CMV infection.

claim: Separate CMV haplotypes can be resolved from high-throughput sequencing data.
source: We have recently demonstrated that separate CMV haplotypes can be resolved from high-throughput sequencing data (Cudini et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Sufficient residual sample was available from five families for analysis.
source: Sufficient residual sample was available from the five families analysed here.
evidence: This describes the sample availability for the study.

claim: Samples with >10³ copies/ml were selected to maximize the chance of recovering near full genomes.
source: To maximize the chance of recovering near full genomes, we selected samples reported in the original publication (Roxby et al., 2014) to have >103 copies/ml, as this is the limit at which we generally can generate whole genomes from blood.
evidence: This describes the sample selection criteria for the study.

claim: Four infants were HIV-exposed uninfected (HEU).
source: Of the five mother–infant pairs analysed, four infants were HEU (infants 22, 123, 41, 14), and one was HIV infected (infant 12).
evidence: This describes the HIV status of the infants in the study.

claim: One infant was HIV infected.
source: Of the five mother–infant pairs analysed, four infants were HEU (infants 22, 123, 41, 14), and one was HIV infected (infant 12).
evidence: This describes the HIV status of one infant in the study.

claim: Breast milk samples had greater than 70% genome coverage at depths of 10× or more.
source: While breast milk samples had greater than 70% coverage at depths of 10× or more, the cervical and infant samples were generally of lower depth, likely due to degradation of DNA due to the age and handling of the samples
evidence: This is a finding from the sequencing analysis reported in the manuscript.

claim: Cervical and infant samples were generally of lower sequencing depth than breast milk samples, likely due to degradation of DNA due to the age and handling of the samples.
source: While breast milk samples had greater than 70% coverage at depths of 10× or more, the cervical and infant samples were generally of lower depth, likely due to degradation of DNA due to the age and handling of the samples
evidence: This is an observation from the sequencing data with a speculative explanation.

claim: Genome coverage and mean de-duplicated read depth were directly related to actual CMV genome copy number present in the input material.
source: genome coverage and mean de-duplicated read depth were directly related to actual CMV genome copy number present in the input material (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the sequencing analysis shown in a figure.

claim: Samples with genome coverage of less than 20% were removed from subsequent analysis.
source: For all subsequent analysis, we removed samples with genome coverage of less than 20%.
evidence: This describes a methodological decision in the data analysis.

claim: Fourteen of the remaining 20 cervical and baby samples had genome coverage above 70% and read depths of greater than 10×.
source: Fourteen of the remaining 20 cervical and baby samples had genome coverage above 70% and read depths of greater than 10× (Table 1).
evidence: This is a summary of the sequencing quality metrics from Table 1.

claim: Sequences from families 12, 14, and 41 all clustered by family.
source: Sequences from families 12, 14, and 41 all clustered by family.
evidence: This is a finding from the multidimensional scaling analysis of CMV genomic sequences.

claim: Families 22 and 123 clustered in two distinct spaces, suggesting infection with more than one strain.
source: Families 22 and 123 clustered in two distinct spaces, suggesting infection with more than one strain.
evidence: This is a finding from the multidimensional scaling analysis with an interpretation.

claim: In all five cases, the first sample from each infant clustered most closely with that of its mother, indicating the likelihood of recent maternal–infant transmission.
source: In all five cases, the first sample from each infant (indicated by an arrow) clustered most closely with that of its mother, indicating the likelihood of recent maternal–infant transmission.
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis with an interpretation about transmission.

claim: A nucleotide diversity of 0.005 or above is likely to indicate a mixed infection.
source: It has previously been reported that a nucleotide diversity of 0.005 or above is likely to indicate a mixed infection (Cudini et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Almost all the breast milk samples were highly diverse and therefore likely to contain multiple virus strains.
source: Figure 2—figure supplement 1 shows that almost all the breast milk samples were highly diverse and therefore likely to contain multiple virus strains, a finding consistent with previous analyses of breast milk from HIV-infected women (Suárez et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the nucleotide diversity analysis shown in a figure and supported by a citation.

claim: The cervical and infant samples, with the exception of one cervical sample from family 12, showed lower diversity.
source: In contrast, the cervical and infant samples, with the exception of one cervical sample from family 12, showed lower diversity.
evidence: This is a finding from the nucleotide diversity analysis.

claim: Computed nucleotide diversities are robust down to sequencing depths of >10.
source: We used subsampling to demonstrate that computed nucleotide diversities are robust down to sequencing depths of >10 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the subsampling analysis shown in a figure.

claim: Low diversity was also observed in cervical and blood spots with higher coverage and read depths.
source: Low diversity was also observed in cervical and blood spots with higher coverage and read depths (Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the nucleotide diversity analysis cross-referenced with Table 1.

claim: Haplotypes for each sample tended to cluster by family group.
source: Figure 3 shows that haplotypes for each sample tended to cluster by family group albeit with clear evidence of distinct clusters even within a family, for example family 22.
evidence: This is a finding from the haplotype reconstruction analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: There is clear evidence of distinct clusters even within a family, for example family 22.
source: Figure 3 shows that haplotypes for each sample tended to cluster by family group albeit with clear evidence of distinct clusters even within a family, for example family 22.
evidence: This is a finding from the haplotype reconstruction analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: A subset of the sequence haplotypes within each family had pairwise distances as great as those between unrelated GenBank sequences.
source: The presence of mixed infections within a single family was supported by data showing that a subset of the sequence haplotypes within each family had pairwise distances as great as those between unrelated GenBank sequences (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the pairwise distance analysis shown in a figure.

claim: In no cases did haplotypes from different families fulfil the clustering criterion confirming that haplotypes were not shared between unrelated families.
source: In no cases did haplotypes from different families fulfil our clustering criterion confirming that haplotypes were not shared between unrelated families.
evidence: This is a finding from the haplotype clustering analysis.

claim: A total of 26 genotypes were identified with between 3 and 9 genotypes for each family.
source: From our data, we identified at total of 26 genotypes with between 3 and 9 genotypes for each family (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the genotype clustering analysis.

claim: All five mothers were infected with multiple genotypes in breast milk.
source: All five mothers were infected with multiple genotypes in breast milk.
evidence: This is a finding from the genotype analysis of maternal breast milk samples.

claim: In many cases, genotypes within a single maternal sample were as genetically distant as unrelated database sequences, suggesting the presence of multiple distinct CMV strains.
source: In many cases, genotypes within a single maternal sample were as genetically distant as unrelated database sequences, suggesting the presence of multiple distinct CMV strains (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the genetic distance analysis with an interpretation.

claim: Relative genotype abundances present in breast milk changed over time.
source: Relative genotype abundances present in breast milk changed over time.
evidence: This is a finding from the longitudinal analysis of breast milk samples.

claim: One unique genotype appeared in the breast milk of mother 22 at 6 weeks, disappearing from a subsequent sample.
source: One unique genotype appeared in the breast milk of mother 22 at 6 weeks, disappearing from a subsequent sample (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the longitudinal genotype analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The unique genotype in mother 22 at 6 weeks may have represented a new reinfection or reactivation of pre-existing latent infection.
source: This genotype was genetically distinct not only from other genotypes in family 22 but also from genotypes in all other families, reducing the likelihood that it was a contaminant and may therefore have represented a new reinfection or reactivation of pre-existing latent infection.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the finding about the unique genotype.

claim: All cervical samples showed a single dominant genotype.
source: All cervical samples showed a single dominant genotype (Figure 4), including mother 12, whose sample was more diverse and found to contain low levels of other genotypes.
evidence: This is a finding from the genotype analysis of cervical samples shown in Figure 4.

claim: The data point to compartmentalization of CMV populations between cervix and breast milk.
source: Overall, the data point to compartmentalization of CMV populations between cervix and breast milk.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings about genotype distributions in different anatomical sites.

claim: CMV genomes from individual infant blood spots showed lower diversity.
source: CMV genomes from individual infant blood spots also showed lower diversity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and predominance of one genotype (Figure 4)
evidence: This is a finding from the nucleotide diversity analysis of infant samples.

claim: Infant blood spots showed predominance of one genotype, indicating the likelihood of a bottleneck in mother-to-child transmission.
source: CMV genomes from individual infant blood spots also showed lower diversity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and predominance of one genotype (Figure 4), including samples with good sequence read depth, for example Baby12 DEL and 9M; Baby14 6W, 14W, and 6M; Baby22 14W; and Baby123 10W and 12M (Table 1), indicating the likelihood of a bottleneck in mother-to-child transmission.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the low diversity and single genotype findings in infant samples.

claim: Two infants (families 12 and 123) who tested positive at birth were first infected with the genotype present in the greatest abundance in the cervix.
source: Two infants (families 12 and 123, Figure 1) who tested positive at birth were first infected with the genotype present in the greatest abundance in the cervix (Figure 4 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing infant and maternal cervical genotypes.

claim: The infant from family 22 whose first sample at 2 weeks of age tested positive showed the same pattern as infants 12 and 123, with infection by the cervical genotype.
source: The same pattern was found in a third infant (family 22) whose first sample at 2 weeks of age tested positive (Figure 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, and Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing infant and maternal cervical genotypes.

claim: All three congenitally infected infants were subsequently re-infected with distinct genotypes present in breast milk.
source: Interestingly, all three of these congenitally infected infants were subsequently re-infected with distinct genotypes present in breast milk (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from longitudinal analysis of infant samples compared to maternal breast milk.

claim: Two infants with initially negative tests from birth onwards first became positive at 6 and 10 weeks, respectively.
source: Two infants with initially two (family 14) and three (family 41) negative tests from birth onwards, first became positive at 6 and 10 weeks, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from the longitudinal testing of infant samples.

claim: The genotypes detected in the blood spots from infants 14 and 41 were present in breast milk and differed from the most abundant genotype in cervix.
source: The genotypes detected in the blood spots from both of these infants were present in breast milk and differed from the most abundant genotype in cervix (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing infant genotypes to maternal cervical and breast milk genotypes.

claim: Sample diversity calculations are robust at read depths of ≥5.
source: To determine the degree to which results were affected by the quality of sequence, we subsampled reads of different samples to show that sample diversity calculations are robust at read depths of ≥5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is a finding from the subsampling analysis shown in a figure.

claim: Eight of the 18 blood spots and four of seven cervical samples had mean read depth of ≥10.
source: eight of the 18 blood spots and four of seven cervical samples had mean read depth of ≥10 (Table 1)
evidence: This is a summary of sequencing quality metrics from Table 1.

claim: All cervical and blood spot samples with read depth ≥10 except one were of low diversity.
source: eight of the 18 blood spots and four of seven cervical samples had mean read depth of ≥10 (Table 1) and all except one were of low diversity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the diversity analysis cross-referenced with sequencing metrics.

claim: All of the haplotypes in the 12 month breast milk sample from mother 12 were present for read depths of 22 or more.
source: All of the haplotypes in this sample were present for read depths of 22 or more, with three haplotypes identified even at the lowest read depth.
evidence: This is a finding from the subsampling analysis of a specific sample.

claim: Nine of 10 cervical and blood spot samples from four families with read depths of >20 had either single genotypes or multiple closely related variants.
source: Nine of 10 cervical and blood spot samples from four families with read depths of >20 (Table 1) had either single genotypes or multiple closely related variants (Figure 4), supporting previous conclusions around compartmentalization and transmission bottlenecks (Renzette et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a finding from the genotype analysis that supports previous conclusions cited in the literature.

claim: The sum weighted FST value for the subset of five genotypes that predominated in the cervical samples was not significantly different from other subsets.
source: The sum weighted FST value for the subset of five genotypes that predominated in the cervical samples was not significantly different from other subsets, suggesting overall that genotypes that predominated in the cervix of these women were less closely related than most other comparisons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, black arrow).
evidence: This is a finding from the FST analysis shown in a figure.

claim: The subset of cervical genotypes from mother–baby pairs 12, 22, and 123 had a sum weighted FST with a value greater than 99.6% of the other subsets.
source: Intriguingly, however, the subset of cervical genotypes from mother–baby pairs 12, 22, and 123 had a sum weighted FST with a value greater than 99.6% of the other subsets (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, blue arrow), indicating a strong signal of inter-patient viral convergence.
evidence: This is a finding from the FST analysis shown in a figure.

claim: The cervical genotypes from mother–baby pairs 12, 22, and 123 were from the three mother–baby pairs with proven congenital infection based on first detection of CMV in the baby at ≤2 weeks of age.
source: These genotypes were from the three mother–baby pairs with proven congenital infection based on first detection of CMV in the baby at ≤2 weeks of age, and in whom the baby's genotype was identical to that predominating in cervix.
evidence: This is a description of the clinical characteristics of the three mother-baby pairs.

claim: In mother–baby pairs 12, 22, and 123, the baby's genotype was identical to that predominating in cervix.
source: These genotypes were from the three mother–baby pairs with proven congenital infection based on first detection of CMV in the baby at ≤2 weeks of age, and in whom the baby's genotype was identical to that predominating in cervix.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing infant and maternal cervical genotypes.

claim: The predominant cervical genotypes from mothers 14 and 41 showed low levels of relatedness.
source: In contrast, the predominant cervical genotypes from mothers 14 and 41 showed low levels of relatedness (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, red arrow).
evidence: This is a finding from the FST analysis shown in a figure.

claim: The infant strains from families 14 and 41 were most closely related to those from their mothers' breast milk.
source: The infant strains from 14 and 41 were most closely related to those from their mothers' breast milk (Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing infant genotypes to maternal breast milk genotypes.

claim: The FST analysis identified 19 genes as likely to be contributing to the genetic similarity between congenitally transmitted genotypes from mothers 12, 22, and 123 (FDR < 0.05).
source: The FST analysis identified 19 genes as likely to be contributing to the genetic similarity between congenitally transmitted genotypes from mothers 12, 22, and 123 (FDR < 0.05) (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the FST analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The comparison between congenitally transmitted and other genotypes generally yielded the same genes when the pairwise difference was varied to cluster haplotypes into more or fewer genotypes.
source: The comparison between these congenitally transmitted and other genotypes generally yielded the same genes when the pairwise difference was varied to cluster haplotypes into more or fewer genotypes (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), suggesting that this finding is not an artefact of decisions about haplotype clustering.
evidence: This is a finding from sensitivity analysis shown in a figure.

claim: Breast milk CMV showed high nucleotide diversity.
source: Breast milk CMV showed high nucleotide diversity and, as has been previously reported (Suárez et al., 2019), contained a mixture of viral genotypes
evidence: This is a finding from the nucleotide diversity analysis supported by a citation.

claim: Breast milk contained a mixture of viral genotypes, some of which were as genetically distant from each other as unrelated GenBank sequences and can therefore be considered distinct viral strains.
source: Breast milk CMV showed high nucleotide diversity and, as has been previously reported (Suárez et al., 2019), contained a mixture of viral genotypes, some of which were as genetically distant from each other as unrelated GenBank sequences and can therefore be considered distinct viral strains.
evidence: This is a finding from the genetic distance analysis with an interpretation.

claim: Cervical samples were of low nucleotide diversity and dominated by a single viral genotype.
source: Cervical samples were of low nucleotide diversity and dominated by a single viral genotype that was, with one exception, present in lower abundance in breast milk.
evidence: This is a finding from the nucleotide diversity and genotype analysis.

claim: The single viral genotype dominating cervical samples was, with one exception, present in lower abundance in breast milk.
source: Cervical samples were of low nucleotide diversity and dominated by a single viral genotype that was, with one exception, present in lower abundance in breast milk.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing genotype abundances between cervical and breast milk samples.

claim: The data fit with most but not all previous reports of CMV within-host compartmentalization based on genotyping of subgenomic fragments.
source: Our data fit with most but not all (Puchhammer-Stöckl et al., 2006) previous reports of CMV within-host compartmentalization based on genotyping of subgenomic fragments (Hage et al., 2017; Kadambari et al., 2017; Ross et al., 2011; Renzette et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings with previous literature.

claim: Little evidence was found for widespread new superinfecting or reactivating viruses in these mothers.
source: We found little evidence for widespread new superinfecting or reactivating viruses in these mothers.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the longitudinal maternal data.

claim: Congenital CMV infection genotypes (strains) comprised families of closely related haplotypes, in line with findings from the immunosuppressed RhCMV monkey model.
source: In line with the findings from the immunosuppressed RhCMV monkey model of congenital infection, cCMVi (Vera Cruz et al., 2020) genotypes (strains) comprised families of closely related haplotypes.
evidence: This is a finding from the haplotype analysis compared to a cited animal model.

claim: Unlike the finding for congenitally transmitted gB and gL RhCMV variants, maternal and infant haplotypes were not completely identical in early, potentially congenital CMV infections or in postnatally transmitted viruses from breast milk.
source: However, unlike the finding for congenitally transmitted gB and gL RhCMV variants, even where we found transmission of one genotype, maternal and infant haplotypes were not completely identical either in early, potentially congenital CMV infections or in postnatally transmitted viruses from breast milk.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing maternal and infant haplotypes, contrasted with findings from an animal model.

claim: Haplotypes sampled at different times from maternal breast milk were not conserved, suggesting a measure of de novo mutation in this patient group.
source: Neither were haplotypes sampled at different times from maternal breast milk conserved, suggesting a measure of de novo mutation in this patient group, in line with the previous findings (Sackman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from longitudinal haplotype analysis with an interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: While all mothers had mixtures of genotypes in breast milk, the proportions changed over time for some (families 22 and 41) and remained more stable in others.
source: While all mothers had mixtures of genotypes in breast milk, the proportions changed over time for some (families 22 and 41) and remained more stable in others.
evidence: This is a finding from longitudinal analysis of maternal breast milk samples.

claim: All infants were initially infected with a single genotype, supporting a bottleneck to CMV transmission.
source: While all mothers had mixtures of genotypes in breast milk, the proportions changed over time for some (families 22 and 41) and remained more stable in others. Whether expanding genotypes in mothers 22 and 41 had been recently acquired is not known but would be consistent with incident reinfection. In contrast, all infants were initially infected with a single genotype (Figure 4), supporting a bottleneck to CMV transmission (Cudini et al., 2019; Vera Cruz et al., 2020; Stanton et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a finding from the infant genotype analysis supported by citations.

claim: Apparent reinfection by viruses present in breast milk occurred in all four infants with multiple samples.
source: Apparent reinfection by viruses present in breast milk occurred in all four infants with multiple samples (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from longitudinal analysis of infant samples.

claim: The appearance of a new strain in an infant sampled from birth can confidently be interpreted as a newly acquired exogenous virus rather than reactivation of a previously undetected one.
source: We posit that the appearance of a new strain in an infant sampled from birth can confidently be interpreted as a newly acquired exogenous virus rather than reactivation of a previously undetected one.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the longitudinal infant data.

claim: In all cases, the reinfecting strains were genetically distant from and replaced the previously dominant strain.
source: In all cases, the reinfecting strains were genetically distant from and replaced the previously dominant strain (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the longitudinal genotype analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: This pattern is consistent with immunity against the infants' first CMV strain not being protective against reinfection with antigenically distinct strains.
source: Taken together with the rise and fall of infant CMV viral loads over time (Figure 1), this pattern is consistent with immunity against the infants' first CMV strain not being protective against reinfection with antigenically distinct strains, a concept that can be further tested.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the reinfection findings.

claim: Reinfection with closely related strains appears to occur readily with both human CMV and animal models.
source: Of note, reinfection with the closely related strains also appears to occur readily with both human CMV and animal models (Boucoiran et al., 2018; Hansen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Repeated reinfection with distinct strains may explain the high genetic variability observed between sequential samples in early sequencing studies of CMV genomes from congenitally infected infants.
source: Repeated reinfection with distinct strains may explain the high genetic variability observed between sequential samples in early sequencing studies of CMV genomes from congenitally infected infants (Pokalyuk et al., 2017; Renzette et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings in the context of previous literature.

claim: Infants who tested positive at <3 weeks from birth were congenitally infected by definition.
source: Those infants who tested positive at <3 weeks from birth were congenitally infected by definition (Boppana et al., 1999).
evidence: This is based on the clinical definition of congenital infection supported by a citation.

claim: Congenital CMV infection cannot be formally ruled out in the two infants classified as having postnatal infection, since sensitivity of PCR detection of CMV DNA in newborn blood spots is only approximately 84%.
source: In contrast, we cannot formally rule out cCMVi in the two others who were classified as having postnatal infection, since sensitivity of PCR detection of CMV DNA in newborn blood spots is only approximately 84% (Wang et al., 2015), and newborn saliva or urine were not available.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors, supported by a citation about test sensitivity.

claim: Congenital CMV infection in the two infants with initially negative tests is unlikely given that only a small minority of infants have cCMVi, even among those born to HIV-infected women.
source: However, this is unlikely given that only a small minority of infants have cCMVi, even among those born to HIV-infected women.
evidence: This is an inference based on epidemiological knowledge.

claim: Genotypes in babies with proven congenital CMV infection were highly similar to maternal cervical genotypes.
source: Furthermore, it is striking that genotypes in babies with proven cCMVi were highly similar to maternal cervical genotypes, while those with negative tests for the first 6 weeks of life were not
evidence: This is a finding from comparing infant and maternal cervical genotypes.

claim: Infants with negative tests for the first 6 weeks of life had genotypes that were not similar to maternal cervical genotypes.
source: Furthermore, it is striking that genotypes in babies with proven cCMVi were highly similar to maternal cervical genotypes, while those with negative tests for the first 6 weeks of life were not
evidence: This is a finding from comparing infant and maternal cervical genotypes.

claim: The strains detected later in the blood of infants 14 and 41 were most similar to those in their mothers' breast milk.
source: and the strains detected later in the blood of these two infants were most similar to those in their mothers' breast milk.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing infant genotypes to maternal breast milk genotypes.

claim: A severe genetic bottleneck occurs during CMV transmission from mother to foetus or infant.
source: While it has previously been noted that a severe genetic bottleneck occurs during CMV transmission from mother to foetus or infant (Sackman et al., 2018; Renzette et al., 2013; Mayer et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: It remains unknown whether CMV transmitted/founder virus populations share genotypic features that confer a fitness advantage for establishing an initial infection.
source: it remains unknown whether CMV transmitted/founder virus populations share genotypic features that confer a fitness advantage for establishing an initial infection, such as seen in HIV (Joseph et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The analysis did not show evidence for inter-patient convergence of cervical genotypes per se.
source: Notwithstanding the apparent dominance of one genotype in each of the cervical samples, our analysis did not show evidence for inter-patient convergence of cervical genotypes per se.
evidence: This is a finding from the FST analysis.

claim: The three cervical genotypes that were detected in babies 12, 22, and 123, who were infected at birth showed a higher level of genetic similarity than over 99.6% of other subset comparisons.
source: Rather the three cervical genotypes that were detected in babies 12, 22, and 123, who were infected at birth showed a higher level of genetic similarity than over 99.6% of other subset comparisons and much greater than would be expected by chance (black line) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the FST analysis shown in a figure.

claim: Twelve of the 19 genes with the highest similarity scores are part of the highly diverse RL11 gene family.
source: Twelve of the 19 genes with the highest similarity scores (Figure 5) are part of the highly diverse RL11 gene family.
evidence: This is a finding from the FST analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: RL11 genes form an island of linkage within the otherwise highly recombinant CMV genome.
source: Uniquely, RL11 genes form an island of linkage within the otherwise highly recombinant CMV genome (Lassalle et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Phylogeny of primate CMV RL11 complexes recapitulates the evolutionary history of the cognate host, suggesting it to be a potential driver of CMV co-evolution and speciation.
source: Phylogeny of primate CMV RL11 complexes recapitulates the evolutionary history of the cognate host, suggesting it to be a potential driver of CMV co-evolution and speciation (Lassalle et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: RL11 family proteins influence tissue tropism or are immunomodulatory.
source: It is intriguing that RL11 family proteins influence tissue tropism (Stanton et al., 2010) or are immunomodulatory (Stanton et al., 2010; Cortese et al., 2012; Van Damme and Van Loock, 2014; Pérez-Carmona et al., 2018; Bruno et al., 2016; Gabaev et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The possibility that within-species CMV RL11 gene-family variation may influence within-host viral adaption to different compartments and/or transplacental transmission presents a tractable hypothesis that can now be tested.
source: Together with its functional properties (Table 2) and extreme diversity (Lassalle et al., 2016), the possibility that within-species CMV RL11 gene-family variation may also influence within-host viral adaption to different compartments and/or transplacental transmission presents a tractable hypothesis that can now be tested.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Congenital CMV infection is thought to occur primarily through maternal viremia followed by replication in placental cytotrophoblasts resulting in spread to the foetus.
source: cCMVi is thought to occur primarily through maternal viremia followed by replication in placental cytotrophoblasts resulting in spread to the foetus (Pereira et al., 2017).

claim: The three mothers who transmitted their viruses congenitally had higher cervical viral loads than mothers whose babies become infected postpartum.
source: The three mothers who transmitted their viruses congenitally had higher cervical viral loads than mothers whose babies become infected postpartum (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing viral loads shown in Figure 1.

claim: Women who transmitted CMV in utero had mean cervical CMV viral loads at 38 weeks that were 0.83 log10 copies/ml (SD = 1.0, p=0.02) higher than women who did not transmit CMV in utero.
source: Analysis of data from the whole cohort of mothers confirmed that women who transmitted CMV in utero had mean cervical CMV vial loads at 38 weeks that were 0.83 log10 copies/ml (SD = 1.0, p=0.02) higher than women who did not transmit CMV in utero (data not shown) (Roxby et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the full cohort data, supported by a citation.

evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

source: and that a possible explanation for our findings is that the properties that promote replication to higher titres in genital tissue may also predispose to transplacental infection.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Being born to HIV-infected women is a major risk factor for congenital CMV infection as well as long-term CMV-related complications, whether or not the child acquires HIV.
source: Being born to HIV-infected women is a major risk factor for cCMVi as well as long-term CMV-related complications, whether or not the child acquires HIV (Garcia-Knight et al., 2017; Gompels et al., 2012).

claim: Irrespective of the route of first infection, HEU children frequently acquire repeated infections with different CMV viruses within the first year of life.
source: We show here that, irrespective of the route of first infection, HEU children frequently acquire repeated infections with different CMV viruses within the first year of life.
evidence: This is a finding from the longitudinal analysis of infant samples.

claim: Preliminary evidence suggests that breast milk of HIV-uninfected women may have lower CMV viral loads and carry fewer strains.
source: Preliminary evidence suggests that breast milk of HIV-uninfected women may have lower CMV viral loads and carry fewer strains (Arcangeletti et al., 2015).

source: If this is true, the possibility that HEU, as well as HIV-infected, infants are exposed to greater numbers of CMV strains during infancy when compared with HIV-uninfected infants may provide an explanation for their worse clinical outcomes, a hypothesis that can now be tested in prospective studies.

claim: The study is limited by the small number of subjects.
source: However, the study is limited by the small number of subjects, the fact that all women were HIV-1 infected and the lack of samples and data to absolutely confirm the route of CMV acquisition by these infants.

claim: By reconstructing the individual CMV haplotypes, evidence was found for mixed CMV infection in HIV-infected women.
source: In summary, by reconstructing the individual CMV haplotypes, we found evidence for mixed CMV infection in HIV-infected women, and compartmentalization of viral strains between cervical and breast milk.
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding of the study.

claim: Compartmentalization of viral strains between cervical and breast milk was found.
source: In summary, by reconstructing the individual CMV haplotypes, we found evidence for mixed CMV infection in HIV-infected women, and compartmentalization of viral strains between cervical and breast milk.
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding of the study.

claim: Infants appeared usually to acquire one virus genotype initially, indicating a transmission bottleneck.
source: Infants appeared usually to acquire one virus genotype initially, indicating a transmission bottleneck, though subsequent reinfection with a second virus from maternal breast milk was common.
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding of the study.

source: Infants appeared usually to acquire one virus genotype initially, indicating a transmission bottleneck, though subsequent reinfection with a second virus from maternal breast milk was common.

source: We also found that viruses transmitted congenitally resembled the virus genotypes that were present at highest abundance in cervix, and shared genetic features that distinguished them from CMV strains predominating in breast milk and in the cervices of women whose infants were apparently first infected post-partum.

claim: Congenitally transmitted viruses shared genetic features that distinguished them from CMV strains predominating in breast milk and in the cervices of women whose infants were apparently first infected post-partum.

evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding of the study.

claim: The data provide new testable insights into the pathogenesis of CMV transmission from mothers to their infants.
source: These data provide new testable insights into the pathogenesis of CMV transmission from mothers to their infants, as well as tools to unravel the importance of viral diversity for reinfection and congenital transmission, questions that are central to the development of a vaccine to prevent the global burden of disease due to CMV.
